classes.label: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
classes.why: The rendered response is the proof the payload executed. A payload without a recorded response showing it rendered unescaped is an unproven claim, not a finding.

classes.label: SQL Injection (SQLi)
classes.why: The database error or extracted data in the response proves the injection. A query string alone does not prove the database executed it.

classes.label: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
classes.why: Both halves of the loop are needed: the outbound request the server was made to issue, and the response it received. One without the other leaves the loop unproven.

classes.label: Broken Access Control
classes.why: The response proving the unauthorized access succeeded is the core proof. A request that was never shown to succeed proves nothing.

classes.label: Authentication Bypass
classes.why: The response showing access granted without valid credentials is the proof. A crafted request that was never shown to be accepted is an unproven claim.

classes.label: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
classes.why: The forged request itself is the proof — the attack is the request, not the response. The response is secondary and stays recommended.

classes.label: Reentrancy
classes.why: The call sequence / transaction trace is what proves reentrancy, and it is recorded in evidence notes — the finding schema has no dedicated trace field, so notes carry it (a documented limitation). A PoC alone does not show the reentrant call order.

classes.label: Information Disclosure
classes.why: The disclosed data must appear in a recorded response. A claim that something is disclosed, with no response showing it, is unproven.

classes.label: XML External Entity (XXE)
classes.why: The malicious XML payload (request) and the server response showing the external entity was resolved are both needed: a payload without a recorded response showing file content or an outbound fetch is an unproven claim.

classes.label: Insecure Deserialization
classes.why: The crafted serialized payload and the observed object-state change live in evidence notes — the finding schema has no dedicated payload/state field, so notes carry them (the same limitation as reentrancy's trace). A PoC alone does not show the deserialized object was abused.

classes.label: Path Traversal
classes.why: The traversal payload (request) and the file content returned (response) are both needed: a payload without a recorded response showing a file outside the intended directory is an unproven claim.

classes.label: Business Logic Flaw
classes.why: The proof is the comparison between the legitimate flow and the abused flow, recorded in evidence notes — no single request or response proves a logic flaw; the sequence and its business effect do.

description: Per-class evidence checklists for finding validation (round 40; extended with four classes in round 57). Each class names the evidence items a finding of that class must carry for a 'valid' verdict (required) and the items a reviewer still checks but which do not gate the verdict (recommended). The generic checklist is the round-31/32 fallback: it is what every finding gets when its vulnerability_type matches no class. Checklist items are presence checks only — they verify that a piece of evidence EXISTS, never that it is true or sufficient. Item predicates live in src/analysis/validator.js (ITEM_CHECKS); an item name in this file that has no predicate is a load error.
